structured_output.hypothesis: If Thompson is right, the great majority of species have a germ-nucleus (haploid) chromosome number between 6 and 16, with species below 6 few and species above 16 fewer still.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Across species in CCDB (one value per species, the median of its recorded haploid n, using 2n/2 where only 2n is recorded): at least 70% have 6 <= n <= 16, AND the share with n < 6 is below 15%, AND the share with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Fewer than 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16, OR the share with n > 16 is greater than or equal to the share with n < 6, OR the share with n > 16 is 15% or more.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'chromosomes in the germ-nuclei' means the reduced (haploid, gametic) number n, not the somatic 2n. Taken to be per species, with each species counted once. 'Few' is operationalised as under 15% and 'fewer still' as a strictly smaller share than the lower tail. A limitation of the plan: the single chosen dataset covers plants only, so it decides the plant arm of a claim about 'plants and animals'. An animal arm would need a separate karyotype database and is not tested here. Polyploidy was unknown in 1917, so polyploid species are kept in the main analysis. A sensitivity analysis may also be reported with the highest-ploidy records removed, but the verdict rests on the full dataset.

dataset.name: Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB)
dataset.why_it_fits: The CCDB is a community database of plant chromosome numbers. It records gametophytic n and sporophytic 2n counts per taxon, so a per-species haploid-number distribution can be built. Fields used: taxon name, gametophytic number (n), sporophytic number (2n). I did not confirm the download options on the landing page, so access is an assumption. It covers plants only.
